title: pip editable installs silently drift from the clone you think you're editing
summary: When a package is pip-installed with `pip install -e`, `pip show <pkg>`'s "Editable project location" is the actual source of truth for what code runs — not whatever clone you happen to be editing. If you have more than one clone/checkout of the same repo on disk, the CLI can keep behaving 'old' after you push/pull changes elsewhere, because the install points at a different, stale clone entirely.
trigger: Before assuming a code change 'isn't taking effect', run `pip show <pkg>` and check Editable project location matches the clone you actually edited/pulled.

title: assets baked into source code at generation time don't auto-update from their source file
summary: A generated artifact (e.g. ASCII art rendered from an image, then hand-copied into a Python constant) has no build step tying it to its source file. Editing the source file (assci.txt) later does nothing to the baked constant (_GLYPH in banner.py) until someone manually regenerates and re-pastes it. Easy to think 'I updated the source, why didn't the output change'.
trigger: When a file looks like a 'source' for something baked into code, check whether there's an actual build step wiring them together, or just a one-time manual copy — and document which, right next to the baked constant.

title: when a GUI installer needs elevation in a non-interactive shell, grab the tool's portable zip instead
summary: `winget install` for a tool that ships an MSI (e.g. GitHub CLI) can fail silently with exit 1602 ('you cancelled the installation') in a non-interactive/sandboxed session, because the UAC elevation prompt can't be answered. Downloading the project's portable/zip release directly (Invoke-WebRequest + Expand-Archive) and calling the .exe by full path sidesteps the need for elevation entirely, with no admin rights required.
trigger: winget/MSI install failing with an elevation-flavored exit code in an automated/non-interactive context.

title: Python namespace-package shadowing when cwd's parent contains a folder matching the import name
summary: Running `python -c "import X"` (or any script) from inside a directory whose *parent* also contains a folder literally named X can make Python resolve X as an implicit PEP 420 namespace package rooted at the wrong path, shadowing the real installed/editable package. `X.__path__` shows a `_NamespacePath` pointing at the unexpected directory instead of the real one, and `X.__file__` may print `None` or raise on further imports.
trigger: An import behaves unexpectedly (wrong __file__/__path__, or ImportError for a name that should exist) only when run from one specific directory — check whether a folder there shares the package's own name.
